quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
source: Joan Didion, Slouching Towards Bethlehem, On Keeping a Notebook (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968)

evidence.where: An online reprint of the passage from On Keeping a Notebook, fetched this run, which gives the sentence verbatim beginning 'I think we are well advised'; corroborated by two further independent reproductions that continue the paragraph with 'Otherwise they turn up unannounced and surprise us, come hammering on the mind's door at 4 a.m. of a bad night and demand to know who deserted them, who betrayed them, who is going to make amends.'
evidence.edition: Slouching Towards Bethlehem, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968; On Keeping a Notebook is in the second section, Personals
evidence.locator: On Keeping a Notebook, in the closing movement of the essay, shortly before 'It is a good idea, then, to keep in touch, and I suppose that keeping in touch is what notebooks are all about.'

reason: The sentence is Didion's and is quoted here in full rather than in the headless form 'We are well advised', which is how it usually travels; keeping the opening 'I think' is the fidelity test and it passes. I reordered the citation to the house shape, book first and essay as the locator, without changing any fact. Joan Didion does not yet stand anywhere in the year. One caution for the editor: the same line is also proposed in the fiction and essay lane as 08-fict-13, so only one of the two may land.
